intro: Excerpts copied from the live CypherMiner source (C:\APPS\CypherMiner). Each shows the real code behind a capability and explains how it powers that feature. The 59 tools are pure client-side TypeScript — no AI, no server, no network calls; the only Python is an optional FastAPI backend that implements the QI module contract.

snippets.title: The Tool interface — every tool implements this
snippets.feature: Self-registering, drop-in tool modules
snippets.explanation: The single contract the whole app is built on. A tool is just data + two functions: run() turns the form values into a result string (sync or async), and an optional visual() draws a live diagram. name/blurb are Loc {en,pt} pairs, so bilingual support is structural. Because the type fixes the shape, the UI can render any tool generically — the interface IS the catalog.

snippets.title: register() — importing a module adds the tool
snippets.feature: In-memory registry with duplicate protection
snippets.explanation: The registry is just an array. Each tool module calls register() at import time, so simply importing the file (via tools/index.ts) wires it in — no central switch statement. Duplicate ids are warned and ignored. toolsByCategory() and friends are what the sidebar, search and category pages read, so the UI and the catalog can never drift apart.

snippets.title: The registration index — add a tool in one line
snippets.feature: 59 tools self-register on import
snippets.explanation: This file is the only place that knows the full tool list. Each import has the side effect of running that module's register() call. Adding a new tool to CypherMiner is therefore exactly two steps: drop one file into src/tools/<category>/, and add one import line here. main.ts imports './tools' once, and all 59 tools come online.

snippets.title: Live tool runner with async-safe results
snippets.feature: Recompute results on every keystroke; handle Promises
snippets.explanation: The generic engine behind every tool view. It calls tool.run() on each input change, supports both sync strings and Promises (async tools like SHA), and uses a monotonically increasing runToken so a slow async result that arrives after a newer edit is discarded — no flicker, no stale output. Thrown errors render inline with a warning glyph instead of crashing. If the tool defines visual(), it's redrawn with the same values.

snippets.title: The form is generated from tool.inputs
snippets.feature: Auto-built input form for any tool
snippets.explanation: renderInput() maps each ToolInput kind (text/textarea/number/range/select) to the right HTML control, wires its change/input event to update the values bag and re-run the tool, and localises every label and option via loc(). This is why a tool author never writes any DOM code — they declare inputs as data and the shell builds the live, bilingual form for them.

snippets.title: Loc resolution + persisted language toggle
snippets.feature: Whole UI + every tool switches EN/PT instantly
snippets.explanation: The heart of the bilingual design. loc() is called on every Loc {en,pt} pair in the app — UI labels, tool names, blurbs, input labels, select options and educational text — returning the active language with an English fallback. The choice is persisted in localStorage and read on load, so the language survives reloads. setLang() + a full re-render is all it takes to flip the entire interface.

snippets.title: A tool returns localised output via ctx.lang
snippets.feature: Tool results adapt to the user's language
snippets.explanation: Tools receive a ToolContext with the active lang, so even computed output is bilingual. Here the factorizer prints 'is PRIME' / 'é PRIMO' and labels factors in the user's language. Input is sanitised (commas/underscores stripped), validated with a clear thrown error (which the UI shows inline), then parsed as BigInt for arbitrary precision.

snippets.title: Caesar shift + the live cipher wheel
snippets.feature: Caesar cipher with an SVG wheel visual
snippets.explanation: A representative crypto tool. shiftText() does the classic modular alphabet shift, preserving case and passing non-letters through. The tool object declares a textarea, a range slider and an encrypt/decrypt select — and a visual() that renders an SVG cipher wheel (renderWheel) reflecting the current shift, so the diagram animates as you drag the slider. Decryption is just a negative shift.

snippets.title: Native browser hashing via Web Crypto
snippets.feature: SHA-1 / 256 / 384 / 512 with no library
snippets.explanation: An async tool. It uses the browser's built-in crypto.subtle.digest — real, audited SHA implementations with no third-party dependency — then hex-encodes the resulting byte buffer. Because run() returns a Promise, the UI runner's runToken guard ensures the hash for the latest input wins. This is the offline-first principle in action: cryptographic primitives come from the platform, not the network.

snippets.title: Cipher Auto-Solver — IoC + chi-squared
snippets.feature: Fingerprint the cipher and crack simple ones
snippets.explanation: The cryptanalysis showpiece. It computes the Index of Coincidence to guess whether the cipher is mono- or poly-alphabetic, applies regex format heuristics (BINARY/HEX/MORSE/BASE64), then scores all 26 Caesar shifts by chi-squared distance from English letter frequencies and returns the three most English-looking decryptions. All statistics run in the browser on the pasted ciphertext.

snippets.title: Base64 over a UTF-8 byte view
snippets.feature: Unicode-safe Base64 encode/decode
snippets.explanation: Naive btoa(str) breaks on non-Latin characters. This routes through TextEncoder/TextDecoder so the Base64 is taken over the UTF-8 bytes — emoji and accented text round-trip correctly. Invalid decode input is caught and rethrown as a friendly, mode-aware message that the UI surfaces inline.

snippets.title: Morse map + bidirectional translation
snippets.feature: Text ↔ Morse with full punctuation
snippets.explanation: A clean encoding tool: one lookup table covers letters, digits and punctuation, and the reverse table is derived automatically from it with Object.fromEntries — no second table to keep in sync. Letters are space-separated and words are joined with ' / ', the conventional Morse word separator, so the output decodes cleanly back.

snippets.title: Accent-stripping slugify
snippets.feature: URL-friendly slugs from accented text
snippets.explanation: A small but telling text tool. Unicode NFD normalisation decomposes 'Café' into 'Cafe' + a combining accent, which the \p{M} unicode-property regex then strips — so 'Olá, Mundo! Café com Pão' becomes 'ola-mundo-cafe-com-pao'. The separator (hyphen or underscore) is user-selectable, and leading/trailing separators are trimmed.

snippets.title: BigInt factorization (Miller-Rabin + Pollard rho)
snippets.feature: Factor large integers, exactly
snippets.explanation: Real number theory, not float approximations. Miller-Rabin primality testing over a fixed witness set proves primality for the integer range JS BigInt handles, and Pollard's rho finds non-trivial factors of composites; factorize() recurses until everything is prime, then the tool groups repeats as p^e. Everything is BigInt, so there's no precision loss on large inputs.

snippets.title: Exact lottery odds with BigInt combinatorics
snippets.feature: True per-tier odds for 'pick k from n'
snippets.explanation: The lottery odds tool uses the hypergeometric formula: the ways to match exactly j of the drawn numbers is C(k,j)·C(n-k,k-j), over C(n,k) total combinations. Combination counts are computed with exact BigInt (nCrBig) so the totals are precise even for large pools, then converted to '1 in X' odds and a percentage per prize tier, with the jackpot row tagged bilingually.

snippets.title: TF-IDF scoring over the bilingual tool index
snippets.feature: 'Which tool do I need?' answered offline
snippets.explanation: The assistant is a pure in-browser information-retrieval engine. ensureIndex() pre-weights each tool's bilingual name (×5), blurb (×3), category and educational text; queries are normalised (accents stripped), de-pluralised and synonym-expanded. Scoring uses squared IDF so distinctive words dominate, with a gentle 1.3× boost for the tool you're currently viewing. It returns the top matches above a 40% relevance cutoff — zero network calls.

snippets.title: Local vs cloud assistant, chosen by config
snippets.feature: Switch to a hosted assistant with no rebuild
snippets.explanation: Both providers honour the same AssistantProvider contract, so the UI dock is provider-agnostic. getAssistant() reads assistantMode from the runtime config.json: 'local' (the shipped default) uses the offline TF-IDF engine, 'cloud' POSTs to a hosted endpoint expecting the same {text,tools} shape. Switching modes is a config edit, not a rebuild — and API keys stay server-side, never in config.json.

snippets.title: FastAPI app + QI module contract
snippets.feature: Health/version/info so QI Hive can monitor it
snippets.explanation: The optional Python backend on port 8502. It implements the three QI module-contract endpoints so QI Hive Mission Control can monitor CypherMiner like every other ecosystem project, and reads CORS origins from the shared QI registry (with a safe localhost fallback) rather than hardcoding them. The 59 tools don't need this server at all — it's reserved for future heavy/data tools that genuinely can't run client-side.

snippets.title: Runtime config: reconfigure without rebuilding
snippets.feature: Edit config.json on a published site, no rebuild
snippets.explanation: On startup main.ts awaits loadConfig(), which fetches ./config.json with cache:'no-store' (so edits take effect on reload) and merges it over typed defaults. This lets an operator switch the assistant to cloud mode, point the lottery tools at a deployed LotteryWiz, or expand the default sidebar on a published build — purely by editing a JSON file. If the file is absent (e.g. offline first load) the defaults apply silently, preserving the offline guarantee.

snippets.title: App bootstrap — wire the pieces, then mount
snippets.feature: Tools + content self-load, then UI mounts
snippets.explanation: The whole app comes up in a few lines. Importing './tools' triggers all 59 register() calls; importing './content' registers the bilingual educational docs; loadConfig() pulls runtime settings. Crucially it's .finally() (not .then()) so even if config.json is missing offline, the UI still mounts with defaults. mount() then renders the registry-driven interface into #app.
